profiles.name: Rolfe Sedan
profiles.excerpt: Rolfe Sedan brought a six-decade character-acting career to radio, where his precise comic and dramatic voices made him a dependable supporting player.
profiles.bio_html:
Rolfe Sedan was born Edward Sedan in New York City in 1896 and began in vaudeville, theatre and silent film. Although he was already an experienced screen actor, he later recalled that radio was difficult to break into because producers judged him by voice alone rather than by his established face and stage record.

Once established at the microphone, Sedan appeared in programs including Lux Radio Theatre, The Adventures of Ellery Queen, Grand Central Station and The March of Time. His screen career often cast him as clerks, waiters, conductors and other sharply defined supporting characters, and radio used the same precision without the visual shorthand.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 25 Lux Radio Theatre performances credited to Sedan, eight NBC University Theater broadcasts, three each on Escape and Voyage of the Scarlet Queen, two each on Fibber McGee and Molly, Sears Radio Theater and Words at War, plus additional work on Broadway Is My Beat.

profiles.name: Ruth Perrott
profiles.excerpt: Ruth Perrott became one of radio comedy's familiar supporting voices, especially as Katie the maid on My Favorite Husband opposite Lucille Ball.
profiles.bio_html:
Ruth Perrott was born in Minneapolis in 1899 and studied at the University of North Dakota and Carnegie Institute of Technology before moving to New York. Radio eventually became a major part of her professional life, and she developed into a dependable comic character actress.

Her best-known continuing role was Katie, the Cooper family's maid on My Favorite Husband. Perrott worked directly with Lucille Ball, Richard Denning and the writers whose domestic-comedy approach later fed into I Love Lucy. She also appeared on The Judy Canova Show and in dramatic radio, giving her career more range than the single comic role suggests.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 23 My Favorite Husband performances credited to Perrott, 12 Lux Radio Theatre broadcasts, six Escape appearances, four Screen Directors Playhouse episodes, two each on Let George Do It and The Adventures of Philip Marlowe, and additional work on Night Beat and This Is Your FBI.

profiles.name: Sylvia Picker
profiles.excerpt: Sylvia Picker gave Box 13 much of its weekly texture as Suzi, secretary to Dan Holiday and a continuing part of the series from its beginning.
profiles.bio_html:
Sylvia Picker was born in New York City in 1909 and worked in film before radio gave her the role most closely associated with her name. In 1948 she joined the syndicated adventure series Box 13, starring Alan Ladd as former newspaperman Dan Holiday.

Picker played Suzi, Holiday's secretary and the regular contact point for the mysterious assignments that arrived through Box 13. The role required both comic timing and expository clarity, and her continuing presence gave the series a stable relationship around Ladd's changing weekly adventures.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 50 Box 13 performances credited to Picker. That concentrated holding documents nearly the full shape of the continuing role that defines her radio career.

profiles.name: Tom Tully
profiles.excerpt: Tom Tully moved from newspaper work into a major radio and stage career before becoming an Oscar-nominated screen character actor.
profiles.bio_html:
Tom Tully was born in Colorado in 1908, served in the United States Navy and worked as a newspaper reporter before turning to acting. He built substantial experience on Broadway and in radio before Hollywood made his face familiar, giving him a strong dramatic foundation long before his best-known films.

Radio included continuing serial roles as well as anthology and western work. Tully played leading or recurring parts on programs such as Home of the Brave, Life Begins and Stella Dallas, then became a frequent guest on Gunsmoke. His later film career included an Academy Award nomination for The Caine Mutiny.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 12 Gunsmoke performances credited to Tully, ten This Is Your FBI appearances, four each on Tales of the Texas Rangers and The Whistler, three each on Broadway Is My Beat, Columbia Workshop, Escape and Lux Radio Theatre.

profiles.name: Charlie Lung
profiles.excerpt: Charlie Lung was a busy Hollywood radio character actor whose surviving credits span suspense, westerns, police drama and feature-film adaptations.
profiles.bio_html:
Charlie Lung belongs to the large West Coast repertory whose professional record survives mainly through cast lists and recordings rather than extensive personal biography. His credits show steady work across several of Hollywood radio's most demanding dramatic formats.

Lung appeared repeatedly on Escape and Lux Radio Theatre, while westerns and crime programs used him for a wide range of supporting roles. The breadth of those appearances indicates the kind of actor producers relied on when weekly productions required fast, credible character work without star billing.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 14 Escape performances credited to Lung, ten Lux Radio Theatre broadcasts, seven Wild Bill Hickok appearances, four Have Gun, Will Travel episodes, three each on Calling All Cars, Let George Do It and Suspense, and two The Adventures of Frank Race performances.

profiles.name: George Neise
profiles.excerpt: George Neise built a radio career in Chicago before becoming a familiar Hollywood character actor on stage, film and television.
profiles.bio_html:
George Neise began acting in Chicago radio in the late 1930s and also worked in stock theatre before World War II. After serving as a pilot in the United States Army Air Corps, he returned to acting and developed the versatility that made him useful in radio, stage work and later television.

Neise could play authority figures, businessmen, comic foils and villains, and that range carried naturally into network radio. Lux Radio Theatre became the strongest concentration of his surviving GRH work, supplemented by comedy, suspense and detective programs.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 28 Lux Radio Theatre performances credited to Neise, seven The Great Gildersleeve appearances, four The Whistler episodes, two each on A Man Called X, Broadway Is My Beat, Dr. Christian and Let George Do It, plus an additional Barrie Craig performance.

profiles.name: Tom Holland
profiles.excerpt: Tom Holland was a dependable West Coast radio supporting actor whose credits move easily among western, crime and anthology drama.
profiles.bio_html:
Tom Holland is another radio professional whose surviving work is more extensively documented than his personal biography. Cast records place him repeatedly in the Hollywood dramatic community of the 1950s, particularly in westerns and detective programs.

Holland appeared on Wild Bill Hickok, The Adventures of Frank Race, This Is Your FBI and Roy Rogers, while anthology programs used him as part of the same flexible repertory pool. His value lay in reliable supporting work rather than a single continuing star role.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 11 Wild Bill Hickok performances credited to Holland, nine The Adventures of Frank Race appearances, five This Is Your FBI episodes, four Sears Radio Theater broadcasts, three Roy Rogers appearances and additional work on Broadway Is My Beat, NBC University Theater and Screen Directors Playhouse.

profiles.name: Virginia Christine
profiles.excerpt: Virginia Christine built a substantial radio and screen career before becoming nationally familiar as Mrs. Olson in the long-running Folgers commercials.
profiles.bio_html:
Virginia Christine was born in Stanton, Iowa in 1920 and began her professional career in radio and stage work before moving into film. Her command of accents and dialects made her useful across several media, and she developed into a durable character actress in both dramatic and western material.

Radio placed Christine repeatedly in the repertory surrounding Gunsmoke and Have Gun, Will Travel. Later, television advertising made her one of the most recognizable commercial performers in America as Mrs. Olson in Folgers Coffee spots, a role she played for many years. That sustained sponsor work is substantial enough to retain as a second professional category.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 33 Gunsmoke performances credited to Christine, 12 Have Gun, Will Travel appearances and additional work on CBS Radio Workshop, Fort Laramie, NBC University Theater and The Railroad Hour.

profiles.name: John McGovern
profiles.excerpt: John McGovern was a flexible radio repertory actor whose surviving GRH work is especially strong in science fiction and mid-century network drama.
profiles.bio_html:
John McGovern belongs to the New York and network radio repertory whose professional presence is clearer in cast records than in later biographical summaries. His surviving credits cross literary adaptations, westerns, anthology drama and science fiction.

McGovern appeared repeatedly on both Dimension X and X Minus One, two of network radio's central science-fiction series, and later worked on Theater Five. He also appeared in Lux Radio Theatre, NBC University Theater and western programs, showing the range expected from a working dramatic actor.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves seven performances each on Dimension X and X Minus One credited to McGovern, six Theater Five appearances, five Lux Radio Theatre broadcasts, four each on NBC University Theater and Wild Bill Hickok, three Gunsmoke episodes and additional Columbia Workshop work.

profiles.name: Wade Crosby
profiles.excerpt: Wade Crosby gave Frontier Town one of its defining voices as Cherokee O'Bannon, the colorful sidekick to attorney Chad Remington.
profiles.bio_html:
Wade Crosby became best known in radio for the syndicated western adventure Frontier Town. The series followed attorney Chad Remington in the town of Dos Rios, and Crosby played Remington's companion Cherokee O'Bannon.

Crosby gave Cherokee a broad comic personality modeled in part on the speech rhythms of W. C. Fields, providing a strong contrast to the more straightforward heroism of Jeff Chandler and later Reed Hadley as Remington. The character was not simply incidental comic relief; Cherokee was part of the continuing partnership that gave the series its recognizable sound from episode to episode.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 48 Frontier Town performances credited to Crosby. That concentrated holding provides a substantial record of the continuing role for which he is most strongly associated with radio.
